answers.question: I feel ready. Can I go back to 40 miles next week and start speedwork for the 10K?
answers.answer:
Not quite yet, and here is the honest reason. A marathon takes roughly three to four weeks of easy running to fully absorb, even when the legs feel springy. Jumping from 12 mi to 40 mi in one step, with intervals on top, is the classic way to pull a calf or wake up a tendon that was quiet during the taper.

Here is a safer path if you do want to race the Thanksgiving 10K, which sits about four and a half weeks out:

| Week of | Miles | Running |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oct 26 | ~22 | all easy, optional strides |
| Nov 2 | ~30 | easy plus one light stride or hill session |
| Nov 9 | ~36 | one real workout, 10K-pace reps |
| Nov 16 | ~32 | one sharpener, then taper |
| Nov 23 | ~20 | shakeout and race |

Before I lock that in, tell me: are you racing the 10K, treating it as a hard group run, or pointing at something bigger in the spring? The answer changes how aggressive I get in two weeks.

new.analysis:
You followed the recovery plan exactly: three easy runs at 3, 4 and 5 mi, with rest on the other days. That is the right way to come out of a marathon, and the numbers back it up. Easy heart rate dropped about 5 beats for the same pace, pain stayed at zero, and sleep held at 7.5 hours.

The one thing I want to watch is that Sunday run. You ran 9:51/mi at 139 bpm, which is essentially your pre-race easy pace. That is fine as a one-off, but if we are rebuilding, "easy" should feel almost boring for another week or two. Let the heart rate lead, not the pace.

This week I am adding one more run day and a few more miles, with optional short strides mid-week to wake up the legs without taxing anything. No workouts yet, no long run. If the Thanksgiving 10K is the target, we have room to build and sharpen, but I want to hear from you first so we do not guess at the shape of the next month.
